author: Travis
title: KBS Tour 90 Is a Direct Attack on Dynamic Gold Territory, and Kim Braly Knows That Franchise Better Than Almost Anyone
body:
Steel iron shafts don't have a lot of untouched real estate. The fast-swing, low-launch segment is True Temper Dynamic Gold X100 territory, and it has been for the better part of three decades. When KBS announces a shaft built exactly for that player profile, the competitive subtext isn't subtle.

The Tour 90 is KBS's new addition to the Tour family, available in three weight options (90, 95, and 100 grams) in Stiff and X-Stiff, at $34.95 per shaft through certified fitting facilities and premium independent retailers starting April 15. The spec sheet: step-less design, low-bend point, lower launch and reduced spin compared to the existing Tour 80. The target player: faster swing speeds wanting a penetrating flight with tour-level consistency. That description fits a lot of Dynamic Gold X100 bags.

What makes this more than a routine line extension is who is doing the challenging. Kim Braly founded KBS in 2004 after years developing shafts at True Temper, the company that owns the Dynamic Gold franchise. He built that franchise's institutional knowledge from the inside. When KBS enters the fast-swing steel segment at a price point below Project X LZ and Nippon Modus3 Tour 120, it's not a brand guessing at what X100 players want. It's a brand built by someone who helped define what they want.

The pricing is a choice worth noting. $34.95 puts the Tour 90 meaningfully below where Project X and premium Nippon product sit, which is a different market posture than KBS has historically taken with its higher-end offerings. This is not a premium-only play. It's a volume-eligible price at a performance tier that usually commands more. Whether that moves the needle at the fitting counter or just erodes margin depends on how many certified fitting facilities actually stock it and push it. KBS's distribution through fitting channels is an asset here: this shaft doesn't need to win a shelf war at retail, it needs to win a comparison session. That's a more favorable test.

One detail the press release offers without apparent irony: the shaft is called the Tour 90, and it comes in 90, 95, and 100 grams. Naming a product after one of its three available weights is an editorial choice. It's also a very common one in shaft naming, so perhaps not worth dwelling on. What is worth noting is that the 95 and 100 gram builds are where the X100 player actually lives. The 90-gram option reads more like a crossover to the player who wants the Tour's trajectory character without the full weight commitment. That's a legitimate gap in the lineup. KBS is playing two markets with one product name.

The company currently reports shafts in play across all four major tours and 14 tour winners on staff this season. The KBS Tour has been a consistent WITB presence for years, particularly in iron shafts, and that tour credibility matters in the fitting conversation. The DORMIED Index has KBS trending up 18% month-over-month, which is a real signal for a brand at this level of the market: something in the conversation is working. The Tour 90 launch is presumably part of that.

The longer question for KBS is whether this move signals a deliberate effort to close the gap with Dynamic Gold on the premium-performance steel shelf, or whether the Tour 90 is a product that fills a hole in their own lineup without necessarily pulling players away from True Temper. Those are different ambitions with different scorecards. By August, the fitting data from KBS's certified facility network will start to answer that. Braly's history suggests he knows exactly which customer he's after. Whether that customer switches is the only number that matters.
xPost: Founding KBS after building the Dynamic Gold franchise from the inside is the kind of origin story that makes a low-launch steel shaft launch feel less like a product drop and more like unfinished business.

author: Travis
title: Callaway Just Bought Equity in the Company That's Supposed to Fit You for Any Brand's Clubs
body:
Thirty million dollars is not the number that matters here. Callaway leading the round is.

Arccos Golf announced a $30 million Series C this week, bringing its total raised to $60 million. Callaway Golf led the investment and attached a commercial partnership: Arccos's Strokes Gained analytics will now power the data layer inside Callaway's AI fitting recommendation engine, deployed across more than 500 Callaway-authorized fitting locations. The deal restructures what Arccos is, not just what it has.

Since launch, Arccos has operated above the OEM layer. That was the point. Sensors on any grip, data from any club, a platform that could tell a Titleist loyalist they were losing two shots a round with their 7-iron regardless of the badge. That neutrality is what made the 12 billion tracked shots in Arccos's database worth something. Callaway just became a stakeholder in that database. TaylorMade, PING, and Titleist customers wearing Arccos sensors are now contributing shot data to a system that has a Callaway equity partner at the table. The contract language will call this a technical integration. The structural reality is different.

The comparison that earns its place here is TrackMan. TrackMan has stayed independent across two decades of pressure from OEMs, launch monitor competitors, and a technology arms race that has reshaped every corner of equipment fitting. That independence is precisely why it became the universal standard. Every fitting room in every top-100 US retailer runs TrackMan because no one fears a TrackMan recommendation is tilted toward a particular iron set. Arccos has built genuine technology, 250,000 active users, and a dataset no competitor can replicate quickly. It has now traded a portion of the independence that made that dataset credible for capital and distribution. Club Champion and True Spec built category-leading moats on OEM-agnostic positioning. Callaway is using Arccos to build a proprietary data moat from the other direction. Those two strategies are on a collision course, and the fitting consumer is in the middle.

The 250,000 active user figure is worth a second look. For a company twelve years into the market with genuine technology, solid press coverage, and a real performance case, that number reflects a product that has consistently found an enthusiast ceiling it cannot push through. The mass amateur market has not adopted sensor-based tracking at scale, and Arccos has not solved that problem with prior rounds. Sal Syed says the new capital goes to product development and international expansion in the UK, Japan, and Australia. Those are credible use cases. They are also the same targets every golf technology company names. The DORMIED Index shows a 22-point monthly spike, which is the announcement talking, not a shift in underlying trajectory.

What to watch: whether TaylorMade, PING, or Cobra pull their Arccos integrations or quietly let them run. Callaway buying into a platform that collects performance data on competitors' equipment is not a neutral event, and those brands have product managers who read the same term sheets that investors do. If Arccos's cross-brand sensor adoption slows in the next two product cycles, that will be the tell. If it doesn't, it means the fitting data flywheel is valuable enough that even OEM competitors accept the new arrangement. Either outcome reshapes how performance data gets controlled in the fitting category for the next decade.
xPost: Callaway just bought equity in the company fitting golfers for every brand's clubs. That's not a data partnership. That's a structural shift in who controls fitting recommendations.
